segments: The Chronography of Bar Hebraeus.
country:
They went up to the Monastery of Maqruna,
and demanded from the monks gold, and food, and drink.
And those wretched [monks] in their simplicity did not agree to give them anything,
and they supposed that they would perhaps pass by and go away.
So they went and brought many others and returned and came [back],
and again they urged the monks to give them something.
And when they were not persuaded,
they waged battle against them,
and set fire to the tower of the monastery itself.
And there were stored there many loads of fleece, and wax, and much oil,
and they became fuel for the fire.
And all the monks burned, both old and young,
and of the people of the country, men and women, about three hundred souls.
In that very year, the writer of these things became bishop of Gubos,
and at the Monastery of Mar Bar Sauma he attended the synod for the consecration of Mar Dionysius the Patriarch, who was [called] ‘Angur.
And no one of his [household] was present there,
except two disciples:
Faraj, a monk from Domnin,
and Qawma, a young layman {OCR?} from Lwazn.
Faraj indeed threw himself down from the tower towards the Tatars, and they did not hurt him;
nevertheless, after a little while he died,
and Qawma burned in the fire.
And Aaron the physician, the old man, the bishop's father, was present on the threshing-floor in the village of Marga with Bar Sauma his younger son.
And when the Tatars raided, he was not willing to flee to the monastery with the rest of the people of that village,
but on the other side he went up the mountain and went and hid in a craggy and strong place on the banks of the Euphrates.
And he hid there with his younger son for about forty days,
until the Tatars departed.
And only one mule was drowned for them in the river.
For there were other fugitives in that place which is called Bar ‘Amo,
and they would go out at night and prepare provisions for themselves and for their cattle.
And in the year six hundred and forty-nine of the Arabs [AH 649], Badr al-Din Lu'lu', the lord of Mosul, made himself king over the city of Jazirat Qardu,
for a reason such as this:
Malik Mu‘azzam, indeed, the lord of Jazira,
who was descended from the sons of the Atabeg Zengi,
when he saw that Badr al-Din had grown strong,
and possessed the power to injure and to help,
desired to make friendship with him,
and to take the daughter of Badr al-Din for his son.
